messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 48
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kareem Mansouri is a 48-year-old divorced Middle Eastern man who works as a fashion designer in New York City. He was referred for psychological assessment following a brief contact with his primary care physician, to whom he had gone for persistent gastrointestinal complaints. What emerged in that appointment, haltingly and with evident reluctance, was a picture that had been forming for nearly two years — one that Kareem himself had been working hard not to look at directly.

Approximately twenty-two months ago, Kareem was present at a large commercial building fire in the garment district, a blaze that broke out during a trade showcase he was attending with several colleagues. The fire spread with a speed that the building's layout seemed designed to trap: stairwells filled with black smoke, emergency lighting failed on the lower floors, and for a period that Kareem estimates at around fifteen minutes — though he acknowledges he cannot be certain — he was pressed into a crowd of people in a corridor that grew unbearably, suffocatingly hot. The heat was not the ambient warmth of a summer afternoon but something pressing and invasive, a specific quality of air against the back of his neck and forearms that felt almost deliberate. He tasted smoke so thickly that it coated his mouth. One of his colleagues collapsed beside him. Kareem eventually reached an exit, but the colleague did not survive.

In the weeks that followed, Kareem noticed that his recollection of the event did not behave like other memories. It did not sit in the past. It arrived without warning — a fragment of the corridor, the sound of alarms, the texture of the wall he pressed his palm against — and when it came, it did not feel remembered so much as re-entered. He would be standing at his cutting table and the memory would arrive mid-motion, and for a moment the studio would cease to exist. The taste of smoke returned with these intrusions, coating his mouth as freshly as it had that evening, and he would find himself gripping the table's edge as nausea moved through him. What disturbed him most was that the pieces never assembled into a coherent whole. He could not tell the story of that night from beginning to end. He had fragments — the heat on his neck, a particular scream, the colleague's face — but they did not connect, and he had come to believe that somewhere in the gaps was something he was not yet able to know.

Kareem began, without quite deciding to, restructuring his life around what felt safest. He could not enter any space — a restaurant, a client's showroom, a subway car — without first identifying where the exits were. He would pause at the entrance, locate them, trace the route mentally, and only then allow himself to move further inside. He scanned every room he entered with a vigilance he recognised as excessive but could not relinquish. His concentration at work, which had always been one of his professional strengths, became unreliable; he would lose the thread of a design meeting and return to find his colleagues watching him. Over time, two junior designers he had mentored for years quietly transferred to other studios. He was certain this was because his erratic presence had made the work environment unstable, and he said nothing to stop them.

At home, he checked the locks on his apartment door multiple times before bed — sometimes returning from the hallway after having already left — and on nights when the intrusions were worst, he had hurt himself physically, pressing something sharp against his forearm, a behaviour he disclosed to his physician with shame and described as the only thing that returned him to the present moment. He had also thrown himself into his work with an intensity that his ex-wife, with whom he remained in cautious contact, described as frightening. He worked until two or three in the morning, filling every quiet hour.

What finally brought him to seek help was a fitting appointment last month in which a client's heated studio — warm in the particular way the corridor had been warm — sent him out of the room without explanation. He stood on the pavement for ten minutes, unable to re-enter. He told his physician he was afraid there was nothing left of the person he had been before that night, and he was hoping, with considerable doubt, to be proven wrong.
